items.title: Katie Zacharia leaving White House role less than five days into job
items.summary: Her public debut as press secretary ended with a flurry of media criticism about her credentials and preparedness.
items.content:
Figure caption, Trump: New White House press secretary should 'reconsider' job
Katie Zacharia will be leaving her post as White House press secretary, just five days after her shaky public debut.
US President Donald Trump told reporters moments before news of her exit was announced that he had told her "you don't have to do this if you don't want to" and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider".
Zacharia faced heavy criticism for her first press briefing on Tuesday, which lasted less than 15 minutes and included only three questions from reporters.
The 42-year-old spent the days following playing defence, fielding tough questions from news outlets about her credentials and preparedness for the job.
Trump hinted at her impending exit early on Friday afternoon, during an impromptu news conference in front of the Marine One helicopter.
"I said, 'Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don't need this'," Trump said.
"You don't have to be treated this badly," he continued, adding that he believed she had been treated "pretty nastily" by the media.
Hours later, she praised Trump as "kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and the most hardworking man" on X, writing that it had been an honour to work for him.
As the November midterm elections, which will decide who controls the US Congress, draw closer, Democrats are seizing on Zacharia's abrupt departure as a sign of failure in the Republican White House.
"The White House Press Secretary is gone. Maga extremists continue to fall apart," the top Democrat in the House of Representatives, Hakeem Jeffries, posted on X.
Zacharia appeared visibly nervous during her inaugural White House press briefing, in which she read talking points from a notebook, answered only a few questions and referred to her husband as the president.
During the briefing, a reporter asked Zacharia - who had been called an attorney by Trump and others and who graduated from Pepperdine University's law school - about where she passed the bar exam. To practise law in the US, an attorney must be admitted to a state's bar association by passing a rigorous exam.
After intense scrutiny and digging by the media, Zacharia admitted on Thursday that she did not pass the bar exam.
She did say in a statement that she had practised international transaction law in China with the "appropriate credentials".
Questions about her legal credentials became a major talking point throughout the week, with Sean Hannity, from conservative-leaning Fox News, lobbing particularly pointed questions at her during an interview on Thursday.
When she said she had not passed the bar, he replied: "Why didn't you just say, 'I never practiced law?'"
Zacharia also described how quickly she had taken on the press secretary role - having been hired less than a week before her debut - prompting him to ask: "Am I hearing that you think the staff should have better prepped you?"
When she appeared on Fox & Friends, which Trump often watches, on Friday, Zacharia faced a similar line of questioning.
She told the show's hosts that she did not disclose to Trump that she was not an attorney because "those questions weren't asked", saying she was hired for a communications role, not a legal one.
Host Lawrence Jones then asked her: "Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?"
She avoided offering a direct answer but ended by saying: "I hope to be able to build the confidence and trust of everyone around me."
Zacharia's early exit is the quickest among Trump's White House press team.
Anthony Scaramucci left his post as White House communications director after only 10 days during Trump's first term.
"Records are made to be broken," Scaramucci wrote on X on Friday. "But I take no pleasure in other people's pain."
Prior to her appointment as press secretary, Zacharia was a frequent fixture on right-wing US networks such as Fox and Newsmax.
She had a brief stint as a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and worked as a communications adviser for Trump's social media platform Truth Social, according to her LinkedIn.
In her early career, Zacharia worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.

Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the 1st time since 2023
Trump criticized the moving, calling on the Fed to "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES."
The Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Wednesday in an effort to battle back a monthslong surge of inflation set off by the Iran war . The move marks the central bank's first rate increase since July 2023.
The central bank hiked its benchmark rate a quarter of a percentage point, putting interest rates at a level between 3.75% and 4%.
Hours after the announcement, President Donald Trump criticized the move, repeating a call for lower interest rates that he has made on multiple occasions since his return to office last year.
The Federal Reserve Building is the headquarters of the Federal Reserve System and 12 Federal Reserve Banks, in Washington, D.C.
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" Trump said in a social media post.
However later, Trump told ABC News that despite the Fed doing the opposite of what he has demanded he still has confidence in Fed Chair Kevin Warsh.
"I’m relying on Kevin, but he’s got a very tough board," Trump said from the tarmac while traveling to a campaign rally in North Carolina, referring to the 12-member policymaking board. "He's got a board that was put there by a lot of other people, and the interest rates are too high, they’re not appropriate."
Trump insisted the Fed raised rates “only for political reasons” and to hurt him.
“They’re raising the rates to make Trump do as bad as he can possibly do," he said. "The problem they have is that we have the greatest economy in history."
Earlier Wednesday, the board, including Trump-appointed Warsh, voted unanimously in favor of the rate increase.
That current level of interest rates marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but borrowing costs remain well above a 0% rate established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
Iran live updates: Sticker shock woes rise after Saudi refinery stops crude loading
The major stock indexes turned lower after the policy announcement. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down 630 points, or 1.2%, while the S & P 500 dropped 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq ticked down 0.01%.
"The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long," Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday. "The committee’s unanimous vote shows our resolve to achieve price stability on a timelier basis."
The move appears aimed at containing a recent bout of price increases. Global oil prices are hovering near a four-month high and the average price for a gallon of gasoline tops $4.30, according to AAA .
The U.S. economy has shown signs of additional strain in recent days, including a bond selloff that is pushing up borrowing costs for credit cards and mortgages.
The price woes previously divided central bankers eager to contain inflation but reluctant to cool off the economy and weaken the labor market.
The Fed opted to hold interest rates steady at its most recent meeting in July. Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board, however, voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction in a decade.

Warsh, who took the helm of the central bank in May, has vowed to cool off persistently elevated price increases.
"The Fed's predominant focus right now should be on prices," Warsh said in remarks last month at the Fed's annual summer gathering in Jackson Hole, Wyoming.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference following Federal Open Market Committee meetings at Federal Reserve Headquarters, September 16, 2026 in Washington.
Prices rose 3.4% in August compared to a year earlier, maintaining the same level from the prior month, federal government data last week showed.
Inflation stands more than a percentage point higher than the Federal Reserve's target rate of 2%.
Despite a stubborn bout of inflation, the economy remains fairly robust by some measures.
A blockbuster jobs report earlier this month showed employers added 162,000 workers in August, demonstrating continued resilience for the nation's labor market. The economy grew over three months ending in June, defying fear of a downturn triggered by the Iran war.
Fighting in the Middle East kept global crude prices above $105 a barrel as of Wednesday, which amounted to a rise of about 50% since the Iran war broke out in late February.

The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. stands at $4.36, putting it more than $1.30 higher than before the war, AAA data showed.
Record-high diesel prices have raised transport costs for many everyday products, including groceries, clothes and furniture.
The war in Iran, which began with a large-scale U.S.-Israeli attack in the winter, prompted Iran's near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which facilitates one-fifth of global crude supply. Saudi Arabia over the weekend shut down a key pipeline bypassing the strait, which further constrained oil delivery and put upward pressure on prices.

items.title: Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel?
items.summary: A wave of new Latin American leaders reverses measures meant to isolate Israel after its genocidal war on Gaza.
items.content:
Share Why are Latin American countries building closer ties with Israel? on social media
President of Argentina Javier Milei (C) with businessman Stan Polovets (L) and Israel's President Isaac Herzog during the Genesis Prize ceremony in Jerusalem, June 12, 2025 [Lior Mizrahi/Genesis Prize Foundation/Getty]
When Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar announced on October 8 that Colombia would be moving its embassy to Jerusalem, he made sure to point out how important the development was for his country’s diplomatic narrative, and that it heralded warming relations with Latin American governments.
“We will work hard because this is the diplomatic battle over the truth,” Saar said. “And the truth is, Jerusalem was always the capital of one nation.”
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
list 2 of 3 Venezuela and Israel restore consular ties as relations warm
list 3 of 3 Why Latin America’s ‘pink tide’ is taking a stand against Israel
Brazil, Saar went on to say, might soon join Colombia and the growing list of Latin American countries that had moved their embassies to Jerusalem, the disputed city claimed by Israelis and Palestinians as their capital.
Latin America’s relationship with Israel is shifting, as right-wing parties come into power in the region and pro-Israel politicians use their support for the country to rally voters.
Brazil, the largest country in the region, is in the midst of a presidential election campaign in which the relationship with Israel has become a key talking point.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, a left-wing ardent supporter of Palestine, is locked in a close contest with right-wing rival Senator Flavio Bolsonaro. He has sported Israeli flags at campaign rallies and played up his friendship with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The pair are scheduled to take part in a run-off election after Bolsonaro performed surprisingly strongly in the first -round, apparently raising hopes for a detente with Israeli officials like the foreign minister.
Last month, for instance, Colombia and Israel began allowing their citizens to travel visa-free between their countries, yet another signal the newly inaugurated government of Abelardo de la Espriella wants to restore ties that were cut in the wake of Israel’s war on Gaza.
Experts say the realignment with Israel is driven, in part, by new leaders trying to signal they have joined a regional alignment with United States President Donald Trump. But it’s also being fuelled by a massive lobbying effort in which Evangelical Christian groups and Israeli-government-backed organisations in the region have pushed Latin American countries to support Israel.
“It’s not one factor or the other, but a convergence,” said Marta Tawil Kuri, Research Professor at the Center for International Studies at the College of Mexico. “Right-wing leaderships seeking validation from Washington, evangelical bases giving them electoral and ideological grounding, and an Israeli diplomatic offensive that finds fertile ground in Latin America precisely as its image deteriorates elsewhere.”
Colombia’s last leader, Gustavo Petro, severed ties with Israel over what he said was the genocidal war on Gaza. He stopped exporting Colombian coal to Israel, cut military and security cooperation and planned to open a Colombian embassy to Palestine. The former left-wing fighter seemed to take every public opportunity to criticise Israel, even using a trip to New York City for a United Nations summit to take part in a protest against Trump and the war on Gaza.
His successor, de la Espriella, has rapidly reversed Bogota’s stance on Israel since coming to power in August, announcing plans to move his country’s embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem, re-appoint ambassadors and even recognising Israeli control over the occupied Syrian territory of the Golan Heights.
Countries that have recently re-established ties with Israel after a change in government (Al Jazeera) Strong presidential systems and weak, unprofessional diplomatic corps allow new heads of state to quickly pivot on issues such as ties with Israel, said Kuri.
“Unlike the US, where support for Israel has stayed relatively stable across administrations thanks to more consolidated institutions and bipartisan consensus, in much of Latin America foreign policy can swing sharply from one election to the next because that institutional buffer doesn’t exist,” Kuri said.
In 2023, Argentina elected right-wing populist Javier Milei as president, who pledged to move the embassy to Jerusalem, refused to recognise a Palestinian state at the UN and said he was “proud to be the most Zionist president in the world.”
In Bolivia, the leftist administration of Evo Morales, who was president from 2006 to 2019, had refused to have full diplomatic ties with Israel. This continued under the presidency of Luis Arce, who joined other regional left-wing leaders in recalling their ambassadors from Israel after October 7, 2023. When Arce was voted out last year, his replacement Rodrigo Paz promptly reversed that policy.
Soon after coming to office this August, Chilean President Jose Antonio Kast undid his leftist predecessor’s actions against Israel as well, appointing an ambassador to Israel who describes himself as a “proud Zionist”.
Over in Honduras, the left-wing government was replaced by a right-wing leader this January. New President  Nasry Asfura, the grandson of Palestinian immigrants from Bethlehem, similarly reappointed an ambassador to Israel this year.
In August, Venezuela announced it would restore consular relations with Israel, undoing nearly two decades of an antagonistic stance towards Israel under previous leaders Nicolas Maduro and Hugo Chavez.
Besides deciding where to put their embassies, Latin American governments have also sometimes lent support to legal efforts against Israel over the Gaza war. Mexico, Bolivia, Colombia, Brazil, Chile, Belize, Cuba and Nicaragua are among governments that at one point backed South Africa’s genocide case against Israel at the International Court of Justice.
When Flavio Bolsonaro launched his Brazilian presidential campaign last July, he did so standing beside Argentinian President Milei. Some in the crowd waved Israeli flags and watched as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu delivered a video message calling Bolsonaro a friend and a “great champion of the friendship between our peoples”.
Supporters of Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro rally in Sao Paulo on Independence Day, September 7, 2026 (Amanda Perobelli/Reuters) Giving foreign leaders such a prominent role in an election campaign is “unheard of in Latin America,” said Alexander Main, Director of International Policy at the Washington-DC-based Center for Economic and Policy Research. “This did not happen before, at least not so overtly.”
Bolsonaro’s campaign, experts say, is seeking to make itself part of a larger political camp that is led in the hemisphere by Trump and internationally includes Israel. Some received direct endorsements from Trump, such as Colombia’s de la Espriella and Honduras’s Asfura.
They’ve joined new right-wing umbrella groups led by the US, such as the Shield of the Americas , a counter-narcotics security alliance bringing together Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guyana, Honduras, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Trinidad and Tobago. The effort is part of Trump’s policy for the Western Hemisphere that seeks to keep out the influence of other global powers like China.
Members of this Trump-led bloc have helped facilitate controversial US policies to deter migration, such as El Salvador, which is housing third-country deportees for the US. They’ve also chosen to frame their war on narcotics as a new kind of war on terrorism, a zero-sum conflict that is inspired by Israel’s war on the Palestinians, according to Main.
“They find common ground with Israel on a lot of these things,” Main said.
“Before, you had left-wing politicians in these regions that have seen what has happened in Gaza and called that war crimes and human rights abuses,” Main said. “Now you’ve seen, on the other hand, sectors seeing this as an existential fight against a deep-rooted enemy and that merits a kind of war on terror framing.”
Having good relations with Israel could translate into access to key military and security resources as well, Main said, including the use of sophisticated spy software such as Pegasus – which was developed by an Israeli software company – and sales of military jets or training of forces.
The rally in August in Brazil that featured Netanyahu’s video message was also an attempt to win support from a large and influential voter bloc there who see protecting Israel as part of their religious worldview.
The Evangelical Parliamentary Front, a caucus of pro-Israel evangelical legislators, includes more than 40% of the Chamber of Deputies and more than a quarter of the Senate. If they formed a party, the loose alliance would become the third-largest in the country.
“Those constituencies have become increasingly politicised in recent years, to the point it is beneficial for politicians to court them and one of the ways they can do that is rallying behind Israel,” Main said.
Brazil is not the only country seeing this evangelical push to build ties with Israel.
“Evangelicalism — particularly Christian Zionism — is a real and growing factor in countries like Honduras and Guatemala,” Kuri said.
Around 40 percent of the population in those countries are evangelicals and both governments have moved their embassies to Jerusalem.
Groups from the US have also been lobbying on Israel’s behalf.
The Latino Coalition for Israel, led by Florida-based evangelical pastor Mario Bramnick, sends delegations throughout Latin America and has met with leaders in Guatemala, El Salvador, Brazil, Panama, Chile, and Costa Rica.
“Our support for Israel is first and foremost rooted in the Bible, where it was clearly established that God gave the Land of Israel, with Jerusalem as its undivided capital, to the Jewish people as an eternal covenant,” the group says on its website. A spokesperson for Bramnick declined to comment for this story.
In 2025, the Genesis Prize – an Israeli nonprofit launched with a $100 million endowment and Israeli government backing – awarded $1m to Argentinian President Milei for his “unequivocal support of Israel during one of the most difficult times since the founding of the Jewish State”.
Milei took the money and established the Isaac Accords, modelling the effort after the Abraham Accords, a Trump-backed effort to restore diplomatic and economic ties between Israel and the Arab world. The initiative gives grant money for pro-Israel civil society groups in Latin America. It also keeps meticulous track of many of the signalling moves right-wing governments are making in recent months to show their new stance on Israel, from moving embassies to Jerusalem to how they vote on Israel-related resolutions in the United Nations.
The initiative’s latest push? At the end of Netanyahu’s trip to the UN General Assembly in late September – where most of the audience walked out of his speech in protest – he and the leaders of Bolivia, Panama and Paraguay held their own summit. The Israeli leader urged them to join the Isaac Accords, writing on X that he sought to “expand the circle of friendship and partnership with Israel”.

items.content:
The war between the United States and Iran has upended the global oil market by severely disrupting the flow of oil through two critical waterways: the Strait of Hormuz and, in recent weeks, the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Iran is now stepping up attacks on tankers transiting Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, curtailing the volume of oil exiting the region and keeping global crude prices north of $100 a barrel.
There have been 12 reported attacks on vessels in or near Hormuz in the past week, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, which monitors maritime security in the region. And, earlier this week, two cargo ships sank after attacks by unknown projectiles in separate incidents.
Analysts say intensifying attacks by Iran are in response to the large quantities of oil that have managed to exit Hormuz in recent weeks. The US military has led an effective operation to ferry oil across the strait by assisting “dark” transits – tankers sailing with their transponders turned off and shuttling oil to ships waiting in the Gulf of Oman. Meanwhile, Iran continues to struggle to sail its own tankers through the waterway because of a US naval blockade.
The conflict, now in its eighth month, has also widened to include fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi militants in Yemen. The Houthis have targeted Saudi oil tankers transiting the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and, in recent days, launched deadly strikes on Riyadh’s main international airport.
Videos verified by CNN show Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sinking after it was struck by “unknown projectiles” on October 13. Smoke is seen rising from the ship as it takes on water. Later videos and satellite images show cargo scattered in the water in the Strait of Hormuz.
Two cargo ships sunk in Strait of Hormuz as Iran ramps up attacks in run-up to midterms
The crisis will have long-term ramifications on the global oil market, say analysts.
Oil-importing countries increasingly understand they must “structurally reduce their oil consumption” to become less vulnerable to external shocks, Georg Zachmann, a senior fellow at think tank Bruegel, told CNN.
That, alongside other measures, could help “shield (them) from this increasingly uncertain world,” he said.
The Bab al-Mandeb Strait became more strategically important after the war disrupted the neighboring Strait of Hormuz.
At its peak, around 4.5 million barrels of crude per day were exported from the Saudi Red Sea port of Yanbu, with the bulk – about 3 million barrels per day – exiting via Bab al-Mandeb, according to Richard Bronze, co-founder of Energy Aspects. But those flows “collapsed” after the Houthi threat started escalating this summer, he said.
Johannes Rauball, senior crude analyst at Kpler, said that if the Houthis begin threatening ships from all countries, “This would really create another blow for crude markets. It would really push prices higher again, really tighten balances.”
But after an attack last month by drones from inside Iraq on Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline – which pumps crude toward the country’s Red Sea ports – Riyadh pivoted quickly, stepping up crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz via the US military-assisted shuttle operation.
US President Donald Trump said Iran was probably behind the September attack, with Iran-backed militia groups known to operate inside Iraq. Iran’s foreign ministry has “categorically denied” the accusation. The East-West pipeline is now back online, according to several reports .
Asian countries — the biggest buyers of Saudi oil — have borne the brunt of the crisis during the war, but they have adapted by cutting consumption . China has also greatly reduced its imports by tapping into its strategic reserves. The crisis has also pushed some Middle Eastern countries to explore new export routes through yet-to-be-built pipelines.
“The longer this conflict drags on, the less leverage Iran actually has, because other countries are able to create bypass routes,” Rauball, at Kpler, said.
CNN’s Tim Lister, Aida Karimi, Jessie Yeung, Isaac Lee, Teele Rebane and David Goldman contributed reporting.

items.title: Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It? - The Intercept
items.summary: Dems Have an Opportunity to Force an End to the Iran War. Will They Take It?  The Intercept
items.content:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol Building on July 23, 2026, in Washington, D.C.
For months, Democrats have forced Republicans to take vote after vote on President Donald Trump’s unpopular war on Iran. Now those votes could help Democrats retake Congress — and they will immediately have opportunities to follow through on their anti-war rhetoric.
Democratic leaders like House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York have been cagey about their strategy on Iran for the lame-duck period before the next Congress is sworn in on January 3. So far, months of Capitol Hill maneuvering have produced few concrete results. And one path to potential progress for ending the war is laden with risk: threatening a government shutdown.
Opponents of the war say that, with Democrats pushing for support based on their efforts to end to the war, they owe it to voters to put government spending on the line.
“It will certainly demonstrate whether Democrats are willing to stretch themselves and put up a fight and get uncomfortable,” said Hannah Morris, the vice president of government affairs for the liberal, pro-Israel group J Street, which opposes the conflict. “So much of the rhetoric has been about the Iran war.”
Congress Failed Again to Stop Trump’s Iran War. This Group Is Trying Through the Courts.
In the months since the conflict began on February 28, Democrats and the handful of Republicans opposed to the war have poured most of their energy into votes based on the 1973 War Powers Resolution , which limits the president’s power to wage war without congressional approval. In June, they succeeded in securing House and Senate passage of a war powers resolution, but the Trump administration has ignored the vote, arguing the law is unconstitutional.
ICE Raid on Ilhan Omar Shows How Dangerous Two Years of Flailing Trump Could Get
Trump Is Targeting Ilhan Omar. Where’s the Elite Media Outrage?
An Arkansas Mom Obtained Public Records About a New Data Center. Then She Got Sued.
Advocates still believe the Trump administration should be bound by the June resolution, but they concede that other paths may have more teeth.
If they really want to stop the war, Democrats will have to confront questions of timing, divisions within their own caucus, and the risk of a government shutdown.
One prime opportunity could be the December 11 expiration of a spending bill called the continuing resolution that has been funding the government since the last shutdown. Democrats could attempt to attach a rider to the bill prohibiting the use of any of its funds for the Iran war. If that bill does not pass both chambers, the government shuts down.
The process will provide Democrats with rare leverage before the next Congress is sworn in.
Congressional Democratic leaders have not said whether they are willing to risk a shutdown, however. Jeffries did not tip his hand when he was asked during a recent interview with CNN.
“Listen, we'll deal with the appropriations process when we deal with the appropriations process,” he said . “Right now, the mechanism that is in front of us will be to aggressively move war powers resolutions until we end this war in the best interest of the American people.”
Some Democratic candidates in hotly contested races have gone much further than Jeffries, zeroing in on the appropriations issue. Rep. Tom Barrett, of Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, was one of the few Republicans to vote for an Iran war powers resolution. But environmental activist Will Lawrence still attacked him at a recent debate on the issue of war funding.
Morris, who is part of a coalition of groups that have called on Congress to cut off funding for the war, said she is not sure how aggressively Democrats will be willing to pursue the issue during the lame-duck period.
“Will they be willing to shut down the government over this? I don’t have real answers. I think there are a lot of variables here,” she said.
Another option supported by many advocates is the pending debate over the National Defense Authorization Act, the annual Pentagon budget and policy bill. Critics of the war argue that Congress could attempt to insert a provision into the law cutting off authorization for the conflict.
Democrats should be willing to block the bill if it does not include “meaningful restrictions” on the administration’s ability to wage the war, said Hassan El-Tayyab, legislative director for Middle East Policy at the Friends Committee on National Legislation.
“That’s the mandate we’re seeing from the American people,” he said. “They shouldn't pass a massive defense bill while leaving the administration free to pursue yet another open-ended war in the Middle East.”

Vance suggests disagreement with Trump over Iran war
‘Even if you disagree with him on that one issue, you can have that disagreement. And I think I have had that disagreement,’ US vice president says
HAMILTON, Canada US Vice President JD Vance suggested in an interview aired Friday that he may have disagreed with President Donald Trump over the Iran war.
“Even if you disagree with him on that one issue, you can have that disagreement. And I think I have had that disagreement,” Vance said on a political talk show hosted by former White House spokesman Sean Spicer.
Vance was responding to a question about his relationship with political commentator and former Trump ally Tucker Carlson, who has sharply criticized the Iran war, arguing that it serves Israeli rather than American interests and contradicts Trump’s pledge to avoid costly foreign military interventions.
Vance said that Carlson, who has espoused conservative views, was “very, very angry” over the war. “He and I have had that conversation in private, in public. I know how he feels, and I understand,” he said.
“What I've said to Tucker is don't throw the baby out with the bathwater … Aren't closed borders and ending the ridiculous anti-white racial discrimination in our university admissions, aren't these things worth actually acknowledging that Donald Trump has done a lot of good?”

Electrical engineering undergraduate Lloyd Alcorn takes first place at world’s largest chip design competition
Alcorn and Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Assistant Professor Zain Ul Abideen took first place in a competition at the world’s largest conference focused on chip design and electronic design automation.
For nearly a month, Lloyd Alcorn did not touch grass.
The University of Idaho College of Engineering senior spent a significant portion of his summer inside, running computer operations to test, refine and compete in one of the world’s most competitive challenges combining AI and semiconductor design.
Alcorn and Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering Assistant Professor Zain Ul Abideen took first place in the GenAI-Guided Hardware IP Redaction and Red-Teaming Challenge, a security challenge at the 63rd Design Automation Conference (DAC), the world’s largest conference focused on chip design and electronic design automation.
Students entering the semiconductor field need to understand both how advanced chips are designed and how the intellectual property inside them can be protected. This competition gave Lloyd hands-on experience with generative AI, chip-design tools and adversarial security analysis on a real-world problem. That combination is rarely available at the undergraduate level. Zain Ul Abideen
Assistant professor, Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
DAC brings together more than 5,000 researchers, engineers, industry professionals and students to explore the future of semiconductor technology, artificial intelligence and hardware design. As an undergraduate, Alcorn competed alongside teams from academia and industry.
“It was a chance to get my feet wet as an undergraduate student, and I had no idea experiences like this were even possible until I came to U of I,” Alcorn said.
The competition ran from June to July 2026. Students register to participate as red team members, acting as attackers and blue team members ready to defend their systems. Teams meet their objectives independently then submit final results for demonstration at the conference.
DAC brings together more than 5,000 researchers, engineers, industry professionals and students to explore the future of semiconductor technology, artificial intelligence and hardware design. Alcorn and Abideen created a hardware security system embedded within a microchip to obfuscate, or hide, critical information about the chip’s functionality and intellectual property. They also had to build the system without sacrificing the chip’s computing power or performance. The competition was held remotely, with awards presented during the conference.
Microchips made of semiconductor material pass through multiple manufacturing, packaging, testing and distribution facilities, creating opportunities for sensitive information about a chip’s design and capabilities to be exposed or stolen.
“Students entering the semiconductor field need to understand both how advanced chips are designed and how the intellectual property inside them can be protected,” Abideen said. “This competition gave Lloyd hands-on experience with generative AI, chip-design tools and adversarial security analysis on a real-world problem. That combination is rarely available at the undergraduate level.”
Over several summer weeks, Alcorn adapted and tested the protection workflow, verifying that the protected designs continued to operate correctly, and measuring the effects on chip power and timing. He also conducted an AI-assisted adversarial evaluation to determine what information an attacker might still be able to learn from the protected design.
The remote summer competition pitted both sides of hardware security against each other. Blue teams developed methods to conceal sensitive design information, while red teams used generative AI to test whether that information could be reconstructed.
“Research experience at the intersection of hardware design and security requires experienced faculty willing to be patient with someone still learning. That’s what I found at U of I,” Alcorn said.

If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, These 5 Stocks Have a History of Holding Up
Is a market crash coming? That's the question investors are asking as the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) gets closer to ending its fourth year in a row with double-digit gains.
Understandably, a market crash is a scary thought. However, it's part of investing. When you set up your portfolio, keep that in mind and create your stock mix accordingly. When you do your annual review, swap out different stocks based on where you see gaps. And if you haven't done that yet and anticipate a market crash on the horizon, you should make your move now.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Although a market crash can affect even defensive and value stocks, some manage through better than others, and some actually thrive under adverse circumstances. Costco Wholesale (NASDAQ: COST), TJX Companies (NYSE: TJX), Coca-Cola (NYSE: KO), Procter & Gamble (NYSE: PG), and Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT) all have a history of holding up through market crashes.
What's more, they all pay dividends, and Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble, and Walmart are Dividend Kings , meaning they've raised their dividends for at least 50 consecutive years. That's reliability under pressure. Here's how they performed in 2008, 2018, and 2022, when the S&P 500 lost value:
Costco's low prices are a draw all the time, but they become even more valuable under pressure, and that's why the market loves it during a downturn. As inflation persists, rising another 3.7% in September, Costco's sales growth has accelerated, reaching 13% year over year in September.
Image source: Getty Images. That's great news for Costco investors. Costco stock is neck and neck with the market, up 14% year to date, and if there's a correction or crash, it's likely to manage through .
Notice that in the last chart, Costco underperformed the S&P 500. However, it gained 49% the next year, nearly double the index's gain. Often, the resilience is in how quickly the stock bounces back after a downturn.
TJX is an off-price retail chain that buys overstock and off-season merchandise from designer brands. It works with 21,000 vendors and therefore can be very selective about what it buys.
The company sells products at 20% to 60% off retail prices in its 5,200 global stores, and it becomes a magnet for shoppers during periods of inflation or economic distress. Sales increased 4% year over year in the fiscal 2027 second quarter (ended Aug. 1), and earnings per share were up 24%.
TJX barely beat the market in 2008, and that's another example of a lag period -- it gained 81% in 2009, triple the market's rebound.
Coca-Cola is the world's largest beverage company, and the company has developed brands that people love and are willing to pay for. That gives it sticking power despite whatever's happening in the economy. It generally outperforms when the market's having a tough time, because investors know it has a resilient business, and because of its storied dividend, which it has raised for the past 64 years straight.
Coca-Cola stock has been outperforming this year despite the market's rise for similar reasons, and it's up a fantastic 40%, outperforming many hot tech stocks. Sales increased 7% year over year in the second quarter, and EPS rose 16%.
Procter & Gamble makes many of the world's leading household and hygiene brands, such as Tide laundry detergent, Oral-B oral care, and Bounty paper towels. People are willing to pay extra for these products because they feel they're getting good value, and they're essentials people buy no matter what. Procter & Gamble stock soared early in the pandemic, for example, when people were loading up on toilet paper (it makes the Charmin brand).
Procter & Gamble has one of the longest dividend-raise track records, at 70 years, another reason it's valuable in a downturn.
Finally, Walmart is the largest retailer in the world, with almost 11,000 stores, and it reaches 90% of the U.S. population within 10 miles. Its discount prices are even more attractive when people are penny-pinching.
Image source: Walmart. Today, it's also reaching more people with its e-commerce channels. E-commerce sales increased 23% year over year in the 2027 fiscal second quarter (ended July 31), driving total sales growth of 5.9%.
Walmart is also a Dividend King, having raised its dividend annually for the past 53 years.

items.title: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, History Says This Strategy Can Cut Your Portfolio's Recovery Time in Half - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, History Says This Strategy Can Cut Your Portfolio's Recovery Time in Half  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The last few years have been absolutely fantastic for stock investors. The bull market of the last four years has pushed the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.09% ) 116% higher while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -2.15% ) is up an even more impressive 156%.
While the bull market has been strong and supported by stellar earnings growth and improving outlooks, many investors can't help but notice that stock market valuations are particularly high. That's not a sustainable position for stocks: Either earnings have to grow fast enough to bring valuations lower, or stock prices have to come down.
In fact, it's a practical inevitability that stock prices crash 20% or more in the future. The markets move in cycles, and eventually, some event will trigger a big sell-off in the stock market. If you want to position your portfolio to recover in less than half the time it takes for others, here's exactly what you should do.
It doesn't take any groundbreaking portfolio strategy to produce rapid recoveries in the event of a stock market crash. Investors can hold a simple 60/40 stock/bond portfolio with periodic rebalancing and achieve superior results in maintaining portfolio stability.
Since 1988, the 60/40 portfolio has recovered from drawdowns of 20% or more in just 11 months on average, according to data compiled by J.P. Morgan analysts. Meanwhile, the S&P 500 took an average of 24 months to recover, even with dividends reinvested.
It's worth noting that the 60/40 portfolio only stands out against an all-stock portfolio in terms of recovery when the portfolio drops at least 20%. Smaller drops don't exhibit much difference in how long it takes the portfolio to recover. That said, that's exactly the kind of protection an investor should hope for from bonds : a stabilizing force amid big long drops without providing too much drag amid shorter pullbacks.
The stability of the 60/40 portfolio is further evidenced by the likelihood that it will produce a positive return over any given five- or 10-year period. Since 1989, the 60/40 portfolio has produced a positive return 99% of the time over any five-year period and 100% of the time over 10 years. The S&P 500 alone only achieves positive returns 87% of the time over five years and 93% of the time over 10 years.
Maintaining a 60/40 ratio between stocks and bonds in your portfolio requires periodic rebalancing. When more volatile stocks crash, you'll end up with a lower ratio of stocks to bonds in your portfolio. You'll have to sell some bonds and buy some stocks to return the portfolio to the 60/40 balance.
This act of rebalancing means you automatically buy stocks when they go down. The reverse is also true; you'll sell stocks when they climb higher or if bonds decline. That means you can be opportunistic in buying and selling stocks , which ultimately produces more stable returns and helps a portfolio recover quickly after a crash.
While some have concerns about whether bonds can truly act as a good diversifying asset for stocks after both asset classes fell sharply in 2022, that situation was more of an anomaly than a new normal. Bonds produced positive returns in 21 of the last 25 years in which the S&P 500 declined. As such, investors should remain confident that bonds can provide diversification when it matters most.
With bond prices sinking lower in 2026, right now could be an opportune time to increase your allocation to the asset class. The Vanguard Total Bond Market ETF ( BND +0.01% ) , which tracks the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond index, currently offers a yield to maturity of 5.5%.
Splitting a portfolio between the Vanguard bond ETF and the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF ( VOO -1.10% ) can provide significant downside protection and the potential to recover from a market crash more quickly with the help of rebalancing into stocks.
However, investors should understand that bonds have more limited upside than stocks, and they could drag down performance somewhat over the long run. On average, the 60/40 portfolio has produced an annualized return of 9.4% since 1950, versus 11.7% for the S&P 500. That's the price of downside protection. But with bond values sinking lower this year, that downside protection doesn't look as expensive as in the past.

The Iran war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, and the energy portion goes up $50 a week, top economist says
A shopper looks the meat section of a grocery story in Fort Worth, Texas, Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. AP Photo/LM Otero
More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and  adding to the cost  of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the  midterm elections approach .
Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the  fighting disrupts  Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores.
Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September  jump in wholesale prices  suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated.
The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said.
Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead:
BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or  45% above its prewar level , and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said.
Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to  overall inflation  by raising the cost of moving goods.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz  remains dangerous  and constrained, prolonging  uncertainty over oil supplies  and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild.
BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have  raised ticket prices and fees , trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down.
Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates.
Any growth in grocery prices pains Americans after multiple years of food inflation
BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices  can be volatile , and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs.
Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%.
Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after  multiple years of food inflation . Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers.
A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries.
BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027.
“Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said.
Transportation costs add up throughout product supply chains
BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices.
Consumers have felt the higher costs most directly when sending packages. The U.S. Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select, citing increased transportation costs. UPS, FedEx and DHL also impose fuel surcharges on many shipments.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping costs could remain elevated  during the holiday season  even if oil prices ease. Third-party provider AFS Logistics and financial services company TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter and the highest truckload rates since early 2022.
“We expect fuel to drive elevated transportation costs for the foreseeable future,” AFS Logistics CEO Andy Dyer said.
Although UPS and FedEx surcharges could decline if diesel and jet fuel prices fall, changes to carrier surcharge formulas, holiday fees and tight trucking capacity could keep total shipping bills elevated, AFS said.
